orig: Explain why Veeam Kasten treats a namespace as an application, and what that means for how you will scope protection
prop: Explain why Veeam Kasten for Kubernetes treats a namespace as an application, and what that means for how you will scope protection
why: Naming standard: first use of the product name on a page should be the full 'Veeam Kasten for Kubernetes,' with 'Veeam Kasten' after. This lesson's hero blurb never names the product at all, and the objectives list (the first prose mention on the page) drops straight to the short form. Every other lesson opens its blurb with the full name — this is the one page where the pattern breaks. Doesn't affect a demo audience's comprehension, but it's the one naming-standard gap in an otherwise clean course, so it should be closed before this ships as the reference example.

prop: Protecting an application with Veeam Kasten for Kubernetes, which is accomplished by creating a policy, rests on three concepts:
why: Same naming-standard gap as Lesson 02: the hero objectives never name the product, so this sentence is the first prose use of 'Veeam Kasten' on the page, and it should be the full name on first use per the glossary rule. Cosmetic, not a comprehension issue, but worth a consistent pass across all five lessons rather than three-for-five.

orig: the deployment and release information available from Helm v3, and all of the persistent storage resources associated with those workloads, meaning the PersistentVolumeClaims and PersistentVolumes [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.346].
prop: the deployment and release information available from Helm v3 — Helm is Kubernetes' package manager, covered fully in Module 02, so file the term away rather than chasing it now — and all of the persistent storage resources associated with those workloads, meaning the PersistentVolumeClaims and PersistentVolumes [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.346].
why: This is the very first substantive paragraph of the very first lesson, aimed at an audience with zero Kubernetes exposure, and it drops 'Helm v3' as a bare proper noun with no gloss and no signal that it will be explained later. In a live read-aloud this is exactly where a backup admin interrupts with 'wait, what's Helm?' and the presenter has nothing to say except 'hang on, Module 02.' The course already handles this well elsewhere (the hero prereqs box promises every term is 'defined on the spot or deferred to Module 02') — this is the one spot in the opening minutes where that promise isn't kept inline. A four-word parenthetical closes the gap without touching the cited fact.

orig: If the bucket has object locking enabled, set the Enable Immutable Backups toggle [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.315].
prop: If the bucket has object locking enabled, set the Enable Immutable Backups toggle — this is the setting that keeps a restore point from being deleted or overwritten by anyone or anything, including ransomware operating with valid credentials, until its retention expires [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.315].
why: Immutability and ransomware resilience is one of the three value stories this course is supposed to land, and this is the only place in the whole course where the general-purpose immutability toggle for ordinary application backups is introduced — and it's introduced as a bare checkbox with a bucket-setting prerequisite, nothing else. A VDP admin audience cares about this specific checkbox more than almost anything else on the page; it's the line I'd want to slow down on in a demo, and as written there's nothing to slow down for. (Immutability does get a strong ransomware framing later, in Lesson 04's KDR section — but that's a module away and about protecting Kasten's own catalog, not this general location-profile setting. The benefit shouldn't wait that long.)

orig: Veeam Kasten creates Kopia repositories in object store locations, using Kopia as a data mover, which implicitly provides support to deduplicate, encrypt and compress data at rest; Veeam Kasten performs periodic maintenance on these repositories to recover released storage [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.315].
prop: Veeam Kasten creates Kopia repositories in object store locations, using Kopia as a data mover, which implicitly provides support to deduplicate, encrypt and compress data at rest — the three things that keep your object storage bill down and your exported data unreadable in transit and at rest, with nothing to configure or remember; Veeam Kasten performs periodic maintenance on these repositories to recover released storage [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.315].
why: Deduplication, encryption, and compression 'at rest, for free' is a real cost and security story a VDP admin would want repeated back to their own leadership, and as written it's filed as trivia in the middle of a paragraph about repository mechanics. Small addition, but it turns a fact dump into a line worth remembering.

orig: The snapshotter has a floor. Ensure that the csi-snapshotter container for all CSI drivers you might have installed has a minimum version of v1.2.2 [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.103].
prop: The snapshotter has a floor. Ensure that the csi-snapshotter container for all CSI drivers you might have installed has a minimum version of v1.2.2 — below that, the sidecar is missing capabilities Veeam Kasten depends on to create and clean up snapshots reliably, so this is a check to make before your first policy runs, not a diagnosis to reach for after one fails [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.103].
why: This is an orphaned technical requirement: a version number with zero stated consequence. Everything else in this 'two more storage details that bite later' box explains what breaks if you skip it (the cross-cluster name-matching item does); this one doesn't, so a presenter reading it aloud is just reciting a build number. Low-traffic section of the course, hence minor rather than significant, but worth the one added clause for consistency with its neighbor.

orig: Veeam Kasten also supports a more flexible permissions model that scopes a user's permissions to perform actions only within the context of specified applications [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.263].
prop: Veeam Kasten also supports a more flexible permissions model that scopes a user's permissions to perform actions only within the context of specified applications [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.263] — the middle ground between k10-admin's everything and k10-basic's whole namespace, for the case where one team owns several applications inside a namespace they don't otherwise control.
why: This sentence lands right after the four built-in roles have been cleanly explained, table and all — the section is doing well up to this point — and then names a fifth capability, calls it 'more flexible,' and moves on without saying what it actually does or when you'd reach for it instead of the roles just covered. That's the exact shape of a demo stall: a platform team or a VDP admin who just followed the k10-admin / k10-basic / k10-config-view logic hears 'also supports a more flexible model' and asks 'flexible how?' — and the page has already turned the page on them. One clause closes it without inventing anything not already implied by 'scopes... to specified applications.'
